title: 20 Startup Pitches to Read in Pairs, Not Copy Slide by Slide
summary: 20 Startup Pitches to Read in Pairs, Not Copy Slide by Slide
body_markdown:
People save pitch decks as if the next round depends on finding the right layout. The useful reason to save a deck is that it lets you ask what the founder knew when they wrote it. Some decks that look obvious now were trying to make a doubtful claim believable then.


Read these 20 first-party deck examples and pitch accounts in pairs. A few are founders’ descriptions of the pitch rather than the slides themselves; they're labeled accordingly. No single example tells you which slide raised the money.


## Start with a customer job


1. [Intercom: Seed](https://www.intercom.com/blog/first-pitch-deck/) . Ask which bit of the original problem still survives after all the features have changed.
2. [Buffer: Seed](https://buffer.com/resources/the-slide-deck-we-used-to-raise-half-a-million-dollars/) . Put dated product or paying-customer evidence where a reader can find it quickly.
3. [LinkedIn: Series B](https://www.reidhoffman.org/linkedin-pitch-to-greylock/) . Name the critical assumption and point to the evidence you would have needed to believe it then.
4. [Front: Series A](https://front.com/blog/inside-fronts-series-a-slide-deck) . Define the buyer’s familiar workflow before introducing the software category.
5. [Front: Series B](https://front.com/blog/front-series-b-deck) . Compare with the A-stage version: which uncertainty now has a number attached?


## Compare the same business across rounds


1. [Front: Series C](https://front.com/blog/front-series-c-deck) . Practice explaining what evidence improves when customer scale grows.
2. [Front: Series D](https://front.com/blog/front-series-d-deck) . Read this next to the earlier rounds rather than borrowing its expectations for a seed pitch.
3. [Equals: Seed](https://wrap-text.equals.com/p/equals-seed-deck) . Try describing the job a prospective buyer already does inside a tool they know.
4. [Equals: Series A](https://wrap-text.equals.com/p/equals-series-a-deck) . Print the seed and A materials side by side and mark which claims acquired evidence.
5. [Pitch: Series B](https://pitch.com/blog/how-we-built-the-pitch-deck-for-our-85m-series-b) . Consider when the deck is itself a product demonstration and when that would distract from the company.


## Check what the product makes possible


1. [Cube: Series B](https://www.cubesoftware.com/blog/series-b-pitch-deck) . Write down who is accountable for the existing workflow and why they would change tools.
2. [Kestra: Seed](https://medium.com/%40edarras/how-kestra-raised-8m-our-seed-deck-now-public-b3493f5a9fbb) . Explain the old patchwork before introducing technical architecture.
3. [Kestra: Series A](https://medium.com/%40edarras/how-kestra-raised-25m-our-series-a-deck-now-public-8a5b2d625434) . Separate adoption evidence from the business model used to turn adoption into revenue.
4. [Liftit: Series B](https://yupyork.medium.com/liftit-series-b-deck-8531bab24b93) . Name the messy operating step behind the line on the chart.
5. [AppNexus: First pitch](https://review.firstround.com/appnexus-first-pitch-before-it-steered-around-the-cloud-to-win-big-in-adtech/) . Read the first bet as it was at the time, not as a forecast of where the business eventually went.


## Study what changed before the close


1. [Good Audience: Angel](https://medium.com/good-audience/the-fundraising-deck-we-used-to-raise-our-angel-round-af03a519f103) . Match the ask to a plausible next test, not an arbitrary milestone.
2. [PostHog: Early venture](https://medium.com/posthog/how-we-raised-3m-for-an-open-source-project-daf631be2fe0) . Show what open distribution can establish separately from what the company can sell.
3. [Saent: Early fundraising](https://medium.com/en-route-to-saenthood/evolution-of-a-pitch-deck-80a633c77a5) . Keep drafts long enough to see which repeated questions should change your explanation.
4. [Cobot: Series B narrative](https://medium.com/%40bp_64302/cobots-series-b-pitch-narrative-b916b6eb3e6f) . Write the spoken argument first, then see whether every slide earns a place.
5. [Proof Trading: Series A account](https://medium.com/prooftrading/raising-a-series-a-in-2026-8a1cc1604b0c) . Distinguish what the presenter learns about the deal process from what the materials prove about the company.


## Do one more thing before redesigning your deck


Open two pitches for the same company, preferably years apart. Mark three sentences: the reason a customer buys, the reason distribution might repeat, and the risk an investor is being asked to take. Notice which claim the second version can now support with evidence. Notice, too, what never needed a chart.


Then do it to your own pitch. The next revision shouldn't have more slides unless you learned something that gives a reader a better reason to believe you. A faint distinction between who signs the deal and who uses the product is often worth a clearer slide. A new color palette usually isn't.


Finally, check what your stage permits you to claim. A seed slide that shows three accounts doing the same job over and over might show more than a chart showing a projected $50 million. At Series B, the denominator of that retention chart may matter as much as its slope. The specimen you want to study is the one facing a similar uncertainty, not the one that eventually had the biggest outcome.
